A `.csv` file is the right choice when the content is genuinely tabular — rows of records that all share the same fields — and the primary consumer is a program rather than a person. Spreadsheets, pandas/R data frames, SQL `COPY`, and BI tools all read CSV natively, and its strict comma-and-newline structure means parsing needs no custom rules. Its weaknesses are real but bounded: there is no standard way to express types, nesting, formulas, or formatting, so anything richer than a flat rectangle has to be flattened or encoded by convention, and the format is unforgiving of unescaped commas and quotes.

A `.md` file is the right choice when the content is meant to be read by humans and happens to live in a plain-text toolchain. Prose, headings, lists, tables, and links all survive as readable plain text even unrendered, and diffs are line-oriented, which makes Markdown a good fit for docs, READMEs, notes, and long-lived text under version control. Reach for it when structure is narrative or mixed rather than uniform — a Markdown table is fine for a handful of rows in a doc, but once the data grows or needs to be queried, joined, or validated, it should move to CSV and be referenced from the `.md` instead.
